comments.author: DanMcInerney
comments.text: I really don't think any of these SOTA labs are doing agentic engineering correctly. Skills are the universal language of all agent harnesses. If you abstract the taste and prescription out of the skills and into guidance docs, then leave the skills as basically just workflow scaffolding, you can build task-specific workflows that work with any harness like Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, etc. Technically, you only really need 2 skills, work and review, and with these you can build infinitely complex workflows including self-improving loops. I built this out and have been using it for months. It's been extremely nice. https://github.com/DanMcInerney/orchflows

comments.author: otterley
comments.text: If you want people to pay you for your software, stop writing it for free. Conversely, if you write it for free, don't expect people to pay you for it. The original authors of Free Software and open source were career academics and others who were paid to do other things, or were sponsored by scientific and defense research grants. stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、スノーデン文書のリークが現在どのように評価されるべきかということで、「責任ある開示」という概念が薄れつつあるのか、短期的な無責任な開示が長期的には責任ある行動となるのかという意見が交わされた。さらに、過激な監視事実への市民の怒りが持続せず、Epsteinファイルのように時間が問題を薄れさせるという見方や、Overtonウィンドウが移動しかつてのスキャンダルが許容範囲になったという分析も登場した。また、Assangeの例が警告として機能しているのか、あるいはジャーナリストが脅威にさらされて黙らされているのかという懸念も示された。

注目コメントとしては、「Overtonウィンドウが移動し、以前はスキャンダルだったことが許容されるようになった」という指摘が、社会の感覚変化を端的に捉えており、議論の深い洞察として挙げられた。また、「漏らすならどこまでも漏らせ」という簡潔な主張も、情報公開の極端な戦略を示す注目された意見であった。
stories.editor_note: スノーデンアーカイブがその後どうなったかは、監視・プライバシー問題が依然として社会的関心を引く中、日本でも個人データ保護法の改正や政府の監視能力への懸念が高まっており、アーカイブの現状が政策議論や市民運動の材料として再評価されるきっかけとなっています。

comments.author: vunderba
comments.text: So thoughts Positives • It's a heck of a lot smaller than Qwen-Image 1 (20b parameters) at only 7b, making it one of the smaller open-weight models available (Z-Image Turbo is one of the few that is smaller at 6b) when compared to Ideogram, Krea2, Flux2, etc. • It supports native transparency (Qwen's team, as far as I know, is the only one attempting to tackle this). Even though it's relatively trivial to set up background removal postprocessors, it's also neat to see it natively supported. • It's fast using QwenImage2.1 convrot, a 1MP image took around ~5 seconds on an RTX4090. Negatives • The license (assuming you respect it) is far more restrictive. The original Qwen Image 1 was released under the standard Apache license; this one explicitly forbids commercial usage without obtaining a separate license. On the other hand, a lot of us didn't expect the Qwen team to ever release "weights-available" ever again. Qwen-Image 1.0, released about a year ago, only scored 4/15 on my GenAI Showdown Benchmarks . Since that time, they've been upstaged by Krea 2 (6/15) and Ideogram4 (8/15). I'll post the new results once I have some more time to run them. https://genai-showdown.specr.net

comments.author: fasterik
comments.text: I like to think of modern pixel art as its own aesthetic and art form. It's designed to be viewed on high DPI LED screens, and that's fine. I don't think it should be judged by how it looks on a CRT. There's an undeniable charm to the older era of pixel art, and surely part of that is nostalgia, but I also think a lot of it comes from the fact that the economics and the hardware were a lot different. Up until the mid 1990s, the highest paid artists in the industry were working on pixel art games. The hardware was slow enough that there were real creative constraints, and we know that constraints often drive creativity.

comments.author: nayuki
comments.text: > Modern flatscreens all have fixed resolutions True by design. > and purely digital interfaces, True but not relevant. Even if you connected an LCD monitor over an analog interface like VGA or composite video, it would have to re-digitize the signal. The fact that a screen uses a digital interface can be designed independently of whether a screen has fixed pixels (LCD, OLED) or not (monochrome CRT with continuous phosphor, without shadow mask or aperture grille). > ensuring a fixed aspect (width-to-height) ratio True by definition because the pixels are pieces of physical hardware in the screens. > and completely square pixels. This is a design choice. Nothing prevents someone from designing an LCD or OLED matrix with non-square pixels. But there's also no good reason to do so. (Side note: Due to RGB striping, single-color subpixels have an aspect ratio of 1:3, so those are non-square.) Potentially useful trivia: Some image/video formats support declaring the pixel aspect ratio. Examples include PNG ( https://w3c.github.io/png/#11pHYs ) and Matroska.

comments.author: wren6991
comments.text: Speaking to the "uncensored model" angle: there's little reason to distribute abliterated weights anyway. Instead of orthogonalising the weights that write back to the residual stream, you can just orthogonalise the activations themselves. It's equivalent. Orthogonalising activations at runtime is computationally cheap. Just distribute the refusal vectors (few thousand floats per layer), then run against the stock weights. Antirez's DS4 already supports this: https://github.com/antirez/ds4/blob/8db1d1d155cb0400a86a86b9... Abliterated weights are just a bad habit we've gotten into. It's also deeply suboptimal from a precision point of view to take a model that's already been QATed and distributed in pre-quantised form (DeepSeek V4, Kimi K2.5 or K3...), modify its weights, and re-quantise it. Similarly, abliterated models regain some of their refusal behaviour when they're re-quantised after abliteration -- avoidable by keeping the two separate.

comments.author: Sharlin
comments.text: The history of W in Finnish is interesting (for some values of "interesting"). Mikael Agricola [1], a Lutheran clergyman, essentially created literary Finnish from scratch in the 1500s (before that, Finnish had existed solely as a spoken, vernacular language, with official business conducted in Swedish (or German), and until the reformation, the language of the Church had of course been Latin). Agricola had to create an alphabet for Finnish, and naturally borrowed heavily from Swedish and, to a lesser extent, German. His orthography was not particularly self-consistent, and for example the /u/ and /v/ phonemes might be written as either "u", "v", or "w" in Agricola's works. For example, the word uusi (/u:si/; "new") was written by him as "wsi", indeed using "w" as a literal "double-u". The /w/ sound did not exist in spoken Finnish. Over time, Finnish became the almost entirely phonetic language that it is now, with letters matching phonemes essentially one-to-one. /u/ was regularized as "u" and /v/ as "v". As /w/ still doesn't exist, the letter "w" is very rarely used, mainly in some surnames as an alternative spelling of "v"; phonebooks used to collate "v" and "w" as the same letter. In loanwords "w" becomes "v" (e.g. "whiskey" -> viski ). Finns with a thick accent (see "Rally English" [2]) tend to pronounce the foreign /w/ as /v/ when speaking English, similar to Germans. Today, imitation of Agricola's orthography is the Finnish version of "ye olde English", used for humorous or intensifying effect. For example, the word vanha "old" might be spelled "wanha" in the name of an antiques shop. "Wanha" also used to be a standard "old news" reply on IRC, especially to links that had already been pasted by someone (and this became so annoying on some channels that it became a kick-worthy offense). [1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikael_Agricola [2] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rally_English

comments.author: skybrian
comments.text: The villager parable is too egalitarian. That's not really how it worked. For most of history, peasants were sustenance farmers, meaning they grew their own food and if the harvest was bad, they could starve. For them, there was no such thing as insurance and they really needed ways to reduce risk. For example, they'd feast their neighbors so that when times were hard, the neighbors would hopefully help them out in turn. Investing in close-knit relationships isn't like barter - it's more like informal credit. Kinship networks still work something like this today. And this meant they didn't really need money. But how do people who aren't peasants themselves get food? By extracting rents and taxes, in return for protection and certain services, perhaps plowing fields. Local "big men" might take payment in kind, but for a more organized government, they'd collect taxes using money, which gave the peasants incentives to grow and sell food for money. So villages would monetize or demonetize depending on the state of nearby governments. A monetized society allows people who aren't farmers to buy food and cities to exist. Therefore, civilization was built on military force, taxes, and rent extracted from peasants, who were the basis of a mostly agricultural economy. Be glad our civilization isn't built on sustenance farming anymore.

comments.author: 10000truths
comments.text: The need to drop privileges at all is a natural consequence of a process spawning API with inherit-by-default capability semantics. You'd never build a new VM or OS this way if you didn't require compatibility with existing software. The secure solution has always been default-nothing semantics, with whitelisted capabilities granted via explicit arguments in the process spawning API. The closest you can get to that model on Linux is the strict mode in seccomp, which disallows every syscall except read(), write(), exit() and sigreturn(). It's more or less a way to restrict a process to being "pure compute/memory". If the process then wants to poke and prod at the outside world, it can only do so by reading/writing the file descriptors it inherited prior to the seccomp call. You can build a RPC on top of that to emulate the "whitelist", with access control and restrictions/policies enforced by whatever is listening on the other end.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Ogre Battle 64のリコンパイルプロジェクトの合法性と進捗状況。コメントでは、関数の残り割合から99.05％と推定され、すでにプレイやMOD作成が可能だが、自身でROMを用意する必要があると説明されている。これに対して、エミュレータと比べてどの程度グレーゾーンかという法的な疑問が提起され、保存活動としての正当性と著作権侵害のリスクが議論された。賛否については、技術的達成を称賛する声と、ROM配布のグレーエリアへの懸念が対照的に示された。特に注目されたのは、「リコンパイルはエミュレータよりも合法的か？」という質問で、プロジェクトの法的位置付けを考えるきっかけとなった点である。
stories.editor_note: Ogre Battle 64 リコンパイルプロジェクト 99.05%は、過去の名作ゲームを現代ハードウェアで動かす取り組みが、日本のレトロゲーマーやインディー開発者の間で再評価の機会を提供し、オリジナルコードの理解と新規プラットフォームへの移植技術の共有が進んでいます。

comments.author: cesaref
comments.text: I think back in the day (say the late 80s) it became apparent to those in charge that this new IT thing was going to be very important in the workplace, and that it was going to be important to train up people to operate computers. Given those in charge were probably one finger typists if that, and befuddled by technology, they would collectively have decided that computers should be standardised so that learnt skills would be transferrable, and therefore they probably imposed ideas like standardised keyboard layouts. Of course it turned out that the next generation were totally capable of operating computers without any formal training, were totally fine with different operating systems, different keyboard layouts, different applications etc, and so there was probably lots of wasted effort solving a non-existent problem.

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
記事で取り上げられた Mac キーボードの記号やレイアウトについて、コミュニティは大きく以下の三点について議論した。  
1. アイコンとテキストのUI方向性——「アイコンは言語に依らない」という意見と、従来のテキストラベルも有用だという意見が交錯。  
2. 標準化の必要性——企業や教育現場でのトレーニングコスト低減を目的としたキーボードレイアウトの標準化が当時は合理的だったが、実際にはユーザーはそれほど困らなかったという見方が出ている。  
3. 機能キーの省略——AppleがCopy/PasteやUndo/Redoといった基本機能キーを用意しなかったことに対する不満が再燃。

**賛否両論**  
- **アイコン推奨派**：言語 barrier をなくすため、特に国際的デバイスでアイコンが優れているとの見方。  
- **テキスト保持派**：すべてのユーザーにとって直感的とは限らないアイコンもあるため、テキストラベルの併用が望ましいとの意見もある。  
- **標準化賛成派**：当時の企業人materiality を考えれば標準化は妥当だったという立場。  
- **標準化非難派**：実際の利用者は様々なOSやレイアウトに柔軟に対応できたので、無駄な一直線ドライバーだったとの批判もある。

**注目コメント**  
- 「カナダキーボードのEnter記号が好きだ」――矢印が箱の中に入る形状がReturnの本質を視覚化しているとの評価。  
- 標準化を背景にした「1人指打ちの経営者達が押し切った仕様」という皇国臨時論調のコメントが話題をさらげた。
stories.editor_note: 時間に失われたキーシンボル パート2: Mac側は、キーボードレイアウトの変遷が日本語入力やプログラミングにおけるキー配置に影響を与え、特にUS配列とJIS配列の違いが開発者の作業効率に直結するため、歴史的変化を知ることが現場でのカスタマイズに役立ちます。

stories.title_en: Sherline Tools Is Going Out of Business
stories.title_ja: Sherline Toolsは事業を終了する

comments.author: Ccecil
comments.text: Sad news. First, Openbuilds now this. Not a surprise to me though since I am operating in the CNC industry I have seen the same struggles and changes, albeit, from a slightly different perspective. I work with the Smoothieware/Smoothieboard project. It seems, from my observation, that most people are not working with hardware like they were a few years ago. The "homebrew" machines and shadetree makers are becoming few and far between. The lie has been heavily sold to the maker community that you are "wasting your time if you make something yourself" since it is cheaper to offshore even small 3d prints and machining projects. Not only that but people have been convinced that they don't have the ability to make a machine. Instead of spending time learning something new/valuable (i.e. Reprap) it is now popular to just have someone else do it...be it AI or a factory in another country with subsidies that create massive differences in bottom line. The ability to make things at home is disappearing. People cannot/will not learn to make their own machines. Companies that make machines that care about their community and customers are disappearing. Maybe it's by design? I don't know.

comments.author: morio
comments.text: I own a lathe and mill from them, both converted to CNC. Sadly their products have changed little in 30+ years. Their precision parts have a use in some applications but it's vastly overshadowed by the cheap parts available from Asia (including India now). 3D printers, laser cutters and benchtop CNC routers have the taken over the lion share of what hobbyists (and some professionals) used to do with these machines. Mine are just collecting dust while my 3D printers crank out parts every day.

comments.author: abakker
comments.text: There’s some other threads in this discussion bemoaning the lack of diy machine builders…and, I am really unclear how this Sherline issue is related? To me, this is a question of value for money. Sherline products were always interesting, but also nowhere near competitive as machines. With controllers like masso and acorn available, converting a mill like a grizzly, precision Mathews or even a Bridgeport are just way more value for money. The other end of the spectrum is tools like the Langmuir bed mill/router or the avid benchtop routers with available 4 pole spindles. There’s a lot of options, closed loop steppers are sub $100, servos from DMM or teknic are readily available and awesome. Sherline has a product set that just felt like a compromise on everything. In the last decade, I’ve built 3 routers, rebuilt a bed mill, converted a Bridgeport, and am currently building an automated beam saw. All the options in the market are drastically better than they were 15 years ago. It’s sad to see a fixture of the community going out of business, but it also a reflection that the business is different now. Given the many different kits and options available, it just doesn’t make sense to buy small work envelope machines for most people.

comments.author: obscurette
comments.text: My wife is in manufacturing and although not in US, working for a company having production in US, EU, Asia etc. Her 1-minute comments why it's increasingly difficult to produce something in EU and US. Bureaucracy - the levels of it are insane especially in EU, but US is not far behind. The loss of local partners and environment - every little thing you can do locally makes production easier and cheaper. Failure to attract young people – although production is cool, it's not Youtube influencer level cool and industry relies increasingly on older generations. Education - the quality of it is sinking almost all over the world. Insecurity - partly just part of times, but mostly coming from regulation, taxes etc.

One reason why I bought sherline is the company was still in business and creating so many accessories. I guess I'll be trying to buy stuff off of eBay or something like I would have been doing had I bought Chinese stuff. stories.summary_ja: シェラインツールが廃業するニュースに対して、Hacker News のコメントでは「自作機械愛好家の減少」と「製品の古さと価格競争力の欠如」が主な議論点だった。多くのユーザーは、安価なアジア製部品や3Dプリンター、レーザーカッター、ベンチトップCNCルーターの普及により、シェラインの小型工作機械が需要を失ったと指摘。一方で、シェラインのマニュアル機械は精密部品に使える貴重なツールだと擁護する声もあり、特に長年にわたるアクセサリ充実度を評価するコメントが見られた。賛否の分かれ目は「コストパフォーマンス」で、グリズリーやマシューズ、ブリッジポートなどの汎用ミルにマスオやアコーンなどの最新コントローラを組み合わせる方が圧倒的にコスパが良いとし、シェラインは「妥協点の多い製品ライン」だと批判する意見が目立った。注目コメントの一つは、製造業に従う妻の発言で、EU・米国での生産が難しくなる要因として官僚主義の増大、地元サプライヤーの減少、若者の離れ、教育の低下、規制・税による不安定さを挙げ、こうした構造的問題がシェラインの衰退にも影響していると指摘していた。
stories.editor_note: Sherline Toolsは事業を終了するは、精密機械工具の供給減少が日本の工作機械や hobby メイカーに影響を及ぼし、代替ブランドへの移行や自社製ジグの開発が求められる状況を示しており、サプライチェーンの多様化が急務です。

stories.title_en: Prompts aren’t Real
stories.title_ja: プロンプトは現実ではない

comments.author: cortesoft
comments.text: I hope the future of AI isn't this sort, where companies provide the user/customer with an interface to an AI that can do things for the user... I would much prefer that companies instead provide an interface FOR an AI, and the user brings their own AI which connects to that interface. In other words, provide my AI with tools, instead of providing me an AI that uses your tools. That way, my AI can bring all the context it needs, and I can bring all of the settings and knowledge about what I want with me. I don't want a fractured world of tons of AIs i interact with where I have to explain all the fundamental information about what I want and how I work every time. This also has the benefit of sidestepping the issue the essay is talking about. You provide a consistent tool, and the AI weirdness is not your issue anymore. You don't have to worry about solving for all the weird ways people prompt the AI, or the ways they break.

comments.author: roughly
comments.text: One issue with this that we ran into is that it costs actual countable money to run the test suite, which is distinct from anything else I’m used to, so the notion that we’d do enough testing to generate a statistically significant gauge of performance - man, I know it’s correct, but I’m not sure my company will survive the process.

comments.author: stickr
comments.text: As awesome as this is, because as much as I want to create an agent for my customer that is predictable and "deterministic", I can't help but think of how wasteful, expensive and not-fun this is. Good for the author that it's fun for them, but for me it seems like I am in that "monkey ladder banana" experimemt: doing something because others are and the customer is giving me bana... sorry, money for it, convinced it will help him (the money would 100% stop if I started looping prompt optimizations like this). If I have so many tools and MCPs as I do currently, and with each the behavior regresses and changes wildly, it seems I should either merge tools and do more automations and come back to the prompt. (The alternative being training my own model?)

comments.author: mmargenot
comments.text: This was great! When you think about optimizing prompts with GEPA (or comparable methods and tools), do you consider each tool or skill separately? How do you think about the optimization of the system prompt for a large agentic system? I imagine that you do a collection of passes to cover each overlapping set of what you want evaluated, but the system prompt makes all cases dependent on each other. What I’ve done in the past is use the system prompt to extract subjective criteria for an LLM judge (like various system prompt statements that contribute to brand voice) and check individual traces with that for evaluation, but I’d like to move beyond including that in a prompt at all.

comments.author: jdlshore
comments.text: This is an amazing article. The problems it describes are exactly what we found when building a production system that used LLMs to (most of the time) produce reliable results. Extensive tests are necessary, and stakeholders have no idea how their suggestions fail in production. They just see the handful of times they tried something and had it work, not the long tail of cursed results. (“How hard can it be? Why don’t you just…”) We didn’t get to the point of self-built prompts, as the article suggests, but it’s an intriguing idea.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、AIサービスの提供形態で、ユーザーが自身のAIを持ち込み企業はツールのみを提供する「インターフェース FOR アイ」方式を支持する意見と、現在の「インターフェース TO アイ」方式への依存がもたらす不安があること。さらに、プロンプト最適化のためのテストスイートの実行コストが実際に大きく、統計的に有意な評価を得るためのテスト量が企業負担となり、開発の無駄や高コストと指摘された。賛否は、ツールごとに最適化しシステムプロンプトを分離するGEPA等の手法に対し、これが複雑さを増し現実的でないと疑問視する声もある。注目コメントとして、本記事が本番システムでの信頼性問題を的確に捉え、ステークホルダーが表面的成功しか見ず長尾の失敗を見過ごす点を指摘し、自己構築プロンプトへの関心を示した。
stories.editor_note: プロンプトは現実ではないは、生成AIの出力が幻覚やバイアスを含むことを指摘し、日本でも業務でのAI活用が進む中、出力の検証プロセスやヒューマン・イン・ザ・ループの重要性が再認識され、信頼性確保のためのガイドライン策定が進んでいます。

comments.author: drnick1
comments.text: > So the NAS runs Kubuntu 24.04 with ZFS My experience is similar. I no longer use dedicated NAS, firewall, or other exotic distributions. I run plain Debian, and add what I need through standard repo packages. My "NAS" is simply a Samba daemon. The same box runs countless other services including hostapd (WiFi), DNS (Unbound), an email stack (Postfix/Dovecot), multiple game servers, and Podman. > everything else in Docker Compose I would suggest Podman instead. It is far more secure by design (rootless) and is unable to silently alter the firewall's configuration.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、専用NASディストリビューションではなく汎用Debian（またはKubuntu）上にSambaだけを置いてマルチサービス機を構築する手法と、Docker代わりにPodmanを使うべきかという点、さらにUbuntuがZFSサポートを切ることへの懸念、それに加えて小型DC電源の実用性とテスト方法、そしてタッチスクリーンメトリクス表示や自作ダッシュボードの原始性についてである。  

賛否両論として、汎用OS＋Samba派は柔軟性と省電力を評価し、専用NAS派は管理の簡単さを好む。Podman推奨派はrootlessによるセキュリティ向上を挙げ、Docker併用派は互換性とエコシステムの豊富さを指摘。ZFSについて、Ubuntuの方針転換を嘆く声がある一方、代替ファイルシステムへの移行を検討すべきだとする意見もある。  

注目コメントとして、DC電源の過負荷時の挙動やケーブルの耐容量、疑似負荷によるテスト方法、トランジェント対策のコンデンサー追加について詳しく質問したユーザーの投稿が技術的な深さで際立ち、またUbuntuがZFSを削除するという事実に驚きと不安を示したコメントも多くの共感を呼んだ。

stories.title_en: Trying the Software Factory Pattern
stories.title_ja: ソフトウェアファクトリーパターンを試す

comments.author: hibikir
comments.text: Will has trouble with this in a relatively nimble org, where he has good control of what is adopted. Imagine how much fun this is in more ossified enterprise environments, where getting work done efficiently means bypassing process with dev lead and line management blessings. The differences in performance among individuals has never been wider, and not just gains in productivity, but performance losses as some people who have iffy judgement cause trouble a lot faster. Maintaining quality when an organization just lacks the muscle to make changes and nobody has the mandate to try to make sure uptime is in good shape is a challenge. A lot of things break, precisely because there's just as much change as Will sees, but it's very unevenly distriuted.

comments.author: alexpotato
comments.text: So I ended up doing something similar: - Create a Git Hub project board for issues - Connect Grok to the above - Use Grok voice mode to take ideas, have Grok refine them with me and then save them as issues - Created slash commands in OpenCode like /ni (new issue), /do (do an issue), /curr (what is the current issue), /done (self explanatory) - I generally tell the OpenCode instance to /do <number> and then off it goes This give me several benefits: - I can use Grok Voice while walking or driving to develop and test ideas - I can lose my entire local OpenCode setup but still have relevant data in the issues - multiple machines can read from GitHub - I could go even further and have separate user accounts for each of my bots. Having been both a PM, dev, SRE and manager, this really does feel like managing a team of devs.

comments.author: richardbarosky
comments.text: Writing about these things in public and putting yourself out there is greatly appreciated. Hats off for that! However, as far as what's being pursued, it seems more like wantonly trying to ride a hype cycle without strongly questioning the end-to-end value of new software development approaches or vetting their immediate suitability. Personally, I think it would be more sensible to take a few individuals or a smaller team(s) and do more isolated/skunkworks experimentation and adopt as justified based on what those people report/experience. The smaller group can adjust faster and iterate/advise the larger dev org about the good approaches/techniques/strategies, and avoid more broad damage/chaos for things that aren't that well thought out. For more conservative AI use cases like adding to code review, writing low stakes PR summaries, or beefing up security checking, a more global, but still not off-the-rails, approach would be the kinds of things that would make more sense to push more broadly.

comments.author: bsilvereagle
comments.text: Has anyone demonstrably gained market share over a competitor who is vocally _not_ adopting agentic software development flows? This article outlines a lot of process churn without a clear through line to how it is impacting feature development or revenue.

comments.author: bicx
comments.text: My team is in the agentic orchestrator phase. I like this software factory pattern in concept, but our biggest challenges in development are acceptance testing of anything UI-related. Mobile app testing in particular is still a huge bottleneck that requires a human. AI models really suck at identifying poor usability and jank, particularly because they only typically process snapshots of the app from an instance in time. I know there are traditional testing frameworks that can detect jitter and frame drop to a certain level. We could potentially start having agents build that in. If we had concrete designs and specs on every project, that would also be helpful, but in a fast-moving startup, that gets delegated to the builders. That puts a human back in the loop every time. Curious to hear what anyone else does to fully adopt a software factory pattern.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点  
Software FactoryパターンをAIエージェント（Grok）と音声入力で実装し、GitHubプロジェクトボードとOpenCodeのスラッシュコマンドでIssue管理を自動化する試みが話題に。開発速度の向上と分散環境での情報共有の利点が強調された。  

・賛否両論  
賛成側は、声でアイデアを即座にIssue化でき、ローカル環境が壊れてもデータが残り、複数マシンで同期できる柔軟性を評価。反対側は、これが単なるハイプに過ぎず、エンドツーエンドの価値や収益へのインパクトが示されていないとし、まずは小規模なスカンクワークスで検証すべきだと主張。  

・注目コメント  
特に洞察に富む意見として、UI系の受け入れテストはAIが苦手で人間のループが不可欠であり、エージェントがジッターやフレームドロップを検出するテストを組み込む方向性が示された点、そして「エージェントが採用していない競合に市場シェアを奪われた例はあるか」という疑問が指摘された。

人間以外の動物も死への恐れや悲嘆を感じるという観察について、HNユーザーたちが熱く議論した。このニュースは、動物の感情や意識に関する科学的証拠が増えている中で、特に注目された。ユーザーの一人は「驚くべきではない」とし、 mammals（ほやごぶもの）は人間と同様に死に対して恐怖を感じ、同種の仲間が犠牲になる様子に非常に悲嘆を感じると指摘している。

**注目コメント**  
あるユーザーは、「我々人間が他の動物と比べて真に特別なのは言語と計画性くらいだ」とし、「それもAI（人工知能）にとっては通り過せつつある」と指摛。また、「子供を失った親なら誰でも共感できる」というコメントも多くの共感を集めた。
